# Claim index

Each entry: id, claim, verdict, grade, what the research found, limits, a sentence for the manager, and sources. Verified dates are in the repository.

## AI coding tools (AI 编程工具)

### ai-code-quality
- **Claim:** AI tools do not hurt code quality. (AI 工具不会损害代码质量。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / C. The only causal estimate cited here covers a single tool in open-source projects and uses proxy measures. The rest is a vendor report and self-reported survey data.
- **Evidence:** A Carnegie Mellon difference-in-differences study compared 807 GitHub projects that adopted Cursor (January 2024 to March 2025) with 1,380 matched controls. Lines added jumped in the first month and faded within about two months. Static-analysis warnings rose about 30% and code complexity about 40%, and both stayed high. GitClear's vendor analysis of 211 million changed lines (2020 to 2024) reports more copy-pasted code and less moved (refactored) code. DORA 2024 respondents, by contrast, tied 25% more AI adoption to 3.4% higher self-reported code quality.
- **Limits:** Warnings and complexity are proxies, not production defects. The CMU study covers open-source projects and one tool (2024 to early 2025). GitClear measures trends in git history and cannot show cause. DORA's quality figure is self-reported.
- **Say to your boss:** A Carnegie Mellon study of 807 projects found static-analysis warnings up about 30% and complexity up about 40% after Cursor adoption, while the speed gain faded within two months. Let's keep review and lint gates and track rework.
- **Would change the verdict:** Matched or randomized studies of current agents showing no rise in defects, warnings or rework after adoption, ideally in company repositories.
- **Sources:** Hao He, Courtney Miller, Shyam Agarwal, Christian Kästner, Bogdan Vasilescu (2025) Speed at the Cost of Quality: How Cursor AI Increases Short-Term Velocity and Long-Term Complexity in Open-Source Projects https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.04427; GitClear (2025) AI Copilot Code Quality: 2025 Data Suggests 4x Growth in Code Clones https://www.gitclear.com/ai_assistant_code_quality_2025_research; DORA, Google Cloud (2024) Accelerate State of DevOps Report 2024 https://research.google/pubs/dora-accelerate-state-of-devops-2024-report/
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/01-ai.md#ai-code-quality

### ai-code-security
- **Claim:** AI-generated code is as secure as human-written code. (AI 生成的代码和人写的代码一样安全。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / C. Benchmarks show frequent vulnerabilities, but none compares against human code at scale, and the two user studies disagree.
- **Evidence:** In a 2021 test, about 40% of 1,689 programs from GitHub Copilot across 89 scenarios were vulnerable. In a Stanford user study, participants with an AI assistant (codex-davinci-002) wrote significantly less secure code and were more likely to think it was secure. A 58-person C study found AI-assisted users made critical security bugs at a rate no more than 10% higher than controls. Veracode's 2025 vendor benchmark (100+ models, 80 tasks) found 45% of outputs had a known vulnerability; its 2026 updates report about 55 to 56% secure.
- **Limits:** None of these compares AI and human code at scale in production, and humans also write vulnerable code. Tools range from 2021 Copilot to 2025 models, and results vary by language and prompt. Veracode is a vendor report.
- **Say to your boss:** The evidence is thin. Tests find vulnerable output in about 40 to 45% of samples, one user study found AI users wrote less secure code while feeling more sure of it, and another found little difference. Let's keep security review and scanning on AI changes.
- **Would change the verdict:** A large comparison of AI-assisted and human-only code, using current tools and independent vulnerability testing, that finds no difference in flaw rates.
- **Sources:** Hammond Pearce, Baleegh Ahmad, Benjamin Tan, Brendan Dolan-Gavitt, Ramesh Karri (2021) Asleep at the Keyboard? Assessing the Security of GitHub Copilot's Code Contributions https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.09293; Neil Perry, Megha Srivastava, Deepak Kumar, Dan Boneh (2022) Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants? https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.03622; Gustavo Sandoval, Hammond Pearce, Teo Nys, Ramesh Karri, Siddharth Garg, Brendan Dolan-Gavitt (2022) Lost at C: A User Study on the Security Implications of Large Language Model Code Assistants https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.09727; Veracode (2025) 2025 GenAI Code Security Report https://www.veracode.com/resources/analyst-reports/2025-genai-code-security-report/; Veracode (2026) Spring 2026 GenAI Code Security Update https://www.veracode.com/blog/spring-2026-genai-code-security/
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/01-ai.md#ai-code-security

### ai-delivery
- **Claim:** Adopting AI improves software delivery performance. (采用 AI 能提升软件交付表现。)
- **Verdict / grade:** It depends / C. DORA's surveys are large but self-reported and correlational, and the throughput result changed sign between 2024 and 2025.
- **Evidence:** DORA's 2024 survey estimated that a 25% rise in AI adoption went with 1.5% lower delivery throughput and 7.2% lower delivery stability, but also 3.4% higher code quality and 3.1% faster code review. DORA 2025 (nearly 5,000 respondents, 90% using AI) reported a positive link between AI adoption and throughput, and still a negative link with stability. A 2026 NBER working paper (100,000+ GitHub developers) found AI raised coding activity far more than releases.
- **Limits:** DORA data are self-reported survey answers about AI use in general, not one tool generation, so they show association, not cause. The 2024 effects are estimates for a 25% rise in adoption. DORA is run by Google Cloud, which sells AI tools. The NBER paper is a working paper, not peer reviewed.
- **Say to your boss:** DORA found AI adoption linked to lower stability in both years and to higher throughput only in 2025. Faster coding is not faster delivery, so let's watch change failure rate and lead time, not code volume.
- **Would change the verdict:** Controlled or longitudinal data from real organizations showing that AI adoption raises throughput while change failure rate stays flat or falls.
- **Sources:** DORA, Google Cloud (2024) Accelerate State of DevOps Report 2024 https://research.google/pubs/dora-accelerate-state-of-devops-2024-report/; DORA, Google Cloud (2025) 2025 DORA Report: State of AI-assisted Software Development https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/announcing-the-2025-dora-report; Mert Demirer, Leon Musolff, Liyuan Yang (2026) Writing Code vs. Shipping Code: Productivity Effects Across Generations of AI Coding Tools https://www.nber.org/papers/w35275
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/01-ai.md#ai-delivery

### ai-experienced-faster
- **Claim:** AI tools make experienced developers faster. (AI 工具能让经验丰富的开发者更快。)
- **Verdict / grade:** It depends / C. The best randomized trial is small (16 developers) and used early-2025 tools. Its follow-up points to speedups, but its authors call the data unreliable.
- **Evidence:** In METR's randomized trial (early 2025), 16 experienced open-source developers did 246 tasks in their own mature repositories, using Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet. Tasks took 19% longer with AI. A second study from August 2025 (newer tools, 800+ tasks) estimated 18% less time for its 10 returning developers and 4% less for 47 new ones; both intervals include zero. METR says speedups now seem likely but calls the data unreliable, because more developers refused to work without AI. A Science study of about 160,000 GitHub developers (observational) found the gains went to experienced developers.
- **Limits:** METR's setting is narrow: maintainers fixing issues in code they know well. Unfamiliar code, new features and newer agents may give different results. The later estimates come from a self-selected sample, so they cannot settle the question.
- **Say to your boss:** A randomized trial of experienced developers in their own code found early-2025 tools slowed them by 19%. Newer data hint at a speedup, but the researchers call it unreliable. Let's time a few real tasks ourselves.
- **Would change the verdict:** A new randomized trial without the selection problem, using current agents on experienced developers' own repositories, with a confidence interval that excludes zero.
- **Sources:** Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth Barnes, David Rein (2025) Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09089; METR (2026) We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/; Simone Daniotti, Johannes Wachs, Xiangnan Feng, Frank Neffke (2026) Who is using AI to code? Global diffusion and impact of generative AI https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adz9311
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/01-ai.md#ai-experienced-faster

### ai-faster
- **Claim:** AI coding tools make developers faster. (AI 编程工具能让开发者更快完成工作。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Supported / B. Three randomized studies agree on a gain, but sizes range from 21% to 55.8%, they tested earlier tools, and one 2025 trial found a slowdown.
- **Evidence:** In a 2023 preprint, 95 developers wrote an HTTP server in JavaScript, and the GitHub Copilot group finished 55.8% faster. At Google, 96 engineers did one enterprise task and AI cut time by about 21%, with a wide confidence interval. Three field experiments at Microsoft, Accenture and a Fortune 100 firm (4,867 developers) found 26.08% more completed tasks. The 55.8% figure is the high end. Estimates from company settings are lower.
- **Limits:** Studies differ in tool, task and metric, and intervals are wide (standard error 10.3% in the field experiments). The three studies predate today's coding agents. Two other trials found no gain: experienced maintainers in their own repositories (19% slower, 2025) and 52 engineers learning a new library (no significant speedup, 2026).
- **Say to your boss:** Randomized studies find real but modest gains: about 21% less time at Google and 26% more tasks in company trials. The 55% figure comes from one small lab task. Let's plan for a modest gain and measure our own.
- **Would change the verdict:** Repeated randomized trials in real company work that show no gain, or a slowdown, for typical developers using current tools.
- **Sources:** Sida Peng, Eirini Kalliamvakou, Peter Cihon, Mert Demirer (2023) The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06590; Elise Paradis, et al. (2024) How much does AI impact development speed? An enterprise-based randomized controlled trial https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.12944; Zheyuan (Kevin) Cui, Mert Demirer, Sonia Jaffe, Leon Musolff, Sida Peng, Tobias Salz (2026) The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00535; Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth Barnes, David Rein (2025) Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09089; Judy Hanwen Shen, Alex Tamkin (2026) How AI Impacts Skill Formation https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20245
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/01-ai.md#ai-faster

### ai-juniors-more
- **Claim:** AI helps junior developers more than seniors. (AI 对初级开发者的帮助比对资深开发者更大。)
- **Verdict / grade:** It depends / C. Randomized field experiments point one way and a large observational study points the other, with different outcomes and tools.
- **Evidence:** Three field experiments at Microsoft, Accenture and a Fortune 100 firm (4,867 developers, GitHub Copilot) found 26.08% more completed tasks, with higher adoption and larger gains among less experienced developers. A customer-support study (not software) also found novices gained most. A Science study of about 160,000 GitHub developers (Python, through 2024) found the reverse: early-career developers used AI most but showed no measurable gain, while experienced developers captured the gains. METR's 2025 trial studied only experienced developers.
- **Limits:** The two sources measure experience and output differently: the field experiments count completed tasks, while the Science study infers AI use with a classifier on public GitHub code and counts commit activity. Neither measures code quality or learning.
- **Say to your boss:** The studies disagree on who gains more. Controlled experiments inside companies favored less experienced developers; a large GitHub analysis favored seniors. I would not plan headcount on either claim without our own data.
- **Would change the verdict:** A randomized trial that gives AI to both juniors and seniors on the same real tasks and measures completed work and quality.
- **Sources:** Zheyuan (Kevin) Cui, Mert Demirer, Sonia Jaffe, Leon Musolff, Sida Peng, Tobias Salz (2026) The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00535; Simone Daniotti, Johannes Wachs, Xiangnan Feng, Frank Neffke (2026) Who is using AI to code? Global diffusion and impact of generative AI https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adz9311; Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey R. Raymond (2023) Generative AI at Work https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.11771
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/01-ai.md#ai-juniors-more

### ai-learning
- **Claim:** Using AI does not hurt how well developers learn. (使用 AI 不会影响开发者的学习效果。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / B. A randomized trial with developers and a larger one in school math agree, but the developer trial is small and short.
- **Evidence:** Anthropic randomized 52 mostly junior engineers learning the Python library Trio. With a sidebar AI assistant they scored 50% on a later quiz versus 67% without (17 points lower, p = 0.01), with the biggest gap on debugging. They finished only about two minutes faster, not significantly. Those who asked conceptual questions kept more. In a PNAS trial of nearly 1,000 high school students, unrestricted GPT-4 access raised practice scores but hurt later exam results; a guardrailed tutor version largely avoided this.
- **Limits:** One library, a short session, a chat assistant rather than an agent, and a small sample. Harm is not automatic: a study of programming students found no overall effect, and using AI to explain beat using it to write.
- **Say to your boss:** In a randomized trial with developers, people learning a new library with an AI assistant scored 17 points lower on a quiz and did not finish significantly faster. For new hires and new tools, let's use AI to explain, not to write it for them.
- **Would change the verdict:** Randomized trials of current coding agents showing equal or better skill retention on delayed tests in realistic onboarding work.
- **Sources:** Judy Hanwen Shen, Alex Tamkin (2026) How AI Impacts Skill Formation https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20245; Hamsa Bastani, Osbert Bastani, Alp Sungu, Haosen Ge, Özge Kabakcı, Rei Mariman (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2422633122; Matthias Lehmann, Philipp B. Cornelius, Fabian J. Sting (2024) AI Meets the Classroom: When Do Large Language Models Harm Learning? https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09047
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/01-ai.md#ai-learning

### ai-old-studies
- **Claim:** Those AI studies are out of date, because today's tools are much better. (那些 AI 研究已经过时了，因为今天的工具强多了。)
- **Verdict / grade:** It depends / C. The only rerun cited here (METR) is flagged unreliable by its authors. The other newer sources are a working paper and vendor reports.
- **Evidence:** METR now calls its 2025 finding (19% slower with Cursor and Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet) outdated and says speedups seem likely, but its newer data are unreliable because more developers refused to work without AI. A 2026 NBER working paper (100,000+ GitHub developers) found each tool generation (autocomplete, interactive agents, autonomous agents) raised coding activity more, but far less at the level of releases. Veracode's 2026 reports still show about 55 to 56% secure outputs, with no gain from larger models. The learning trial used a sidebar chat assistant, not an agent.
- **Limits:** Newer tools may do better or worse, and no retest with agents is cited here for learning or quality. METR's later estimate and the NBER paper are not peer reviewed, and Veracode is a vendor report. Tie every number to the tool generation it names.
- **Say to your boss:** The 2025 results are dated, and METR says so itself. But the newer evidence is thin and mixed, so let's treat both the old slowdown and the new speedup as unproven and test current tools on our own work.
- **Would change the verdict:** Peer-reviewed randomized trials of current coding agents in company settings that report speed, quality, security and learning outcomes.
- **Sources:** METR (2026) We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/; Mert Demirer, Leon Musolff, Liyuan Yang (2026) Writing Code vs. Shipping Code: Productivity Effects Across Generations of AI Coding Tools https://www.nber.org/papers/w35275; Veracode (2026) Spring 2026 GenAI Code Security Update https://www.veracode.com/blog/spring-2026-genai-code-security/; Judy Hanwen Shen, Alex Tamkin (2026) How AI Impacts Skill Formation https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20245
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/01-ai.md#ai-old-studies

### ai-self-estimate
- **Claim:** Developers can tell whether AI is speeding them up. (开发者自己能判断 AI 有没有让自己变快。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / C. One randomized trial measured both belief and actual time, with only 16 developers, and its result needs more studies to confirm.
- **Evidence:** In METR's 2025 randomized trial, 16 experienced developers expected AI to cut task time by 24% before they started. Tasks done with AI actually took 19% longer. Afterwards the developers still estimated that AI had cut their time by 20%. Belief and measurement pointed in opposite directions. In DORA 2025, over 80% of nearly 5,000 respondents said AI had raised their productivity, but surveys like this record belief, not time.
- **Limits:** Small sample: 16 experienced open-source maintainers working in their own repositories with early-2025 tools. Judgment may be better with newer tools. The trial shows people can be wrong, not that they always are.
- **Say to your boss:** In a randomized trial that checked, developers believed AI saved them 20% of their time while it cost them 19%. Instead of going by feel, let's time a few tasks with and without AI.
- **Would change the verdict:** Several randomized trials in which developers' predicted and measured speedups agree closely, including with current tools.
- **Sources:** Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth Barnes, David Rein (2025) Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09089; DORA, Google Cloud (2025) 2025 DORA Report: State of AI-assisted Software Development https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/announcing-the-2025-dora-report
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/01-ai.md#ai-self-estimate

## Measuring productivity (度量效能)

### measure-commits-per-dev
- **Claim:** Commits or pull requests per developer reveal who performs best. (每位开发者的提交数或 PR 数，能看出谁的表现最好。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / C. We did not find a validation study. This rests on a framework paper and one survey, so it is mostly expert argument.
- **Evidence:** The SPACE authors (Forsgren, Storey, Maddila, Zimmermann, Houck and Butler) treat counts such as commits and pull requests as activity, one of five dimensions of productivity. They say a measurement approach must account for invisible work and for knock-on effects, such as measuring activity at the expense of satisfaction and flow. In a survey of 622 developers at three companies, self-rated productivity was most strongly related to non-technical factors such as job enthusiasm, peer support for new ideas and useful feedback, which a commit count does not show.
- **Limits:** We did not find a study comparing per-developer commit or pull request counts with independent performance ratings, so part of this verdict is absence of evidence. The survey uses self-rated productivity, not manager or peer ratings.
- **Say to your boss:** Commit and pull request counts show activity, and the SPACE authors say any measure has to account for invisible work that counts do not show. I would use the counts to start a conversation, not to rank people.
- **Would change the verdict:** A study linking per-developer commit or pull request counts to independent peer or outcome measures across teams and codebases, and showing the link survives once counts feed into reviews.
- **Sources:** Nicole Forsgren, Margaret-Anne Storey, Chandra Maddila, Thomas Zimmermann, Brian Houck, Jenna Butler (2021) The SPACE of Developer Productivity: There's more to it than you think. https://doi.org/10.1145/3454122.3454124; Emerson Murphy-Hill, Ciera Jaspan, Caitlin Sadowski, David Shepherd, Michael Phillips, Collin Winter, Andrea Knight, Edward Smith, Matthew Jorde (2021) What Predicts Software Developers' Productivity? https://2020.icse-conferences.org/details/icse-2020-Journal-First/10/What-Predicts-Software-Developers-Productivity-
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/02-measure.md#measure-commits-per-dev

### measure-dora-predict
- **Claim:** DORA's four key metrics predict how well a team performs. (DORA 的四个关键指标能预测团队的表现。)
- **Verdict / grade:** It depends / C. Repeated annual industry surveys, but one research program, self-reported on both sides, with little independent replication that we could find.
- **Evidence:** The four keys are deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. In the DORA surveys behind Accelerate, respondents whose teams scored well on them also reported better organizational outcomes. Both the metrics and the outcomes come from survey answers, so this shows association, not forward-looking prediction. Sallin and colleagues note the four metrics are often gathered by hand or by survey with few data points. In DORA's 2024 report the medium cluster had a lower change failure rate than the high cluster, so the cluster labels do not rank teams on every metric.
- **Limits:** One research program, with little independent replication that we could find. The metrics describe software delivery, not business results or developer experience, and are meant to be read as a set.
- **Say to your boss:** The four keys are a useful check on our delivery pipeline, and in DORA's surveys they go with better organizational outcomes. They are not a forecast, and we should read all four together, not chase one.
- **Would change the verdict:** A longitudinal or independently run study showing that changes in the four metrics come before changes in measured business outcomes, after controlling for earlier performance.
- **Sources:** Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble, Gene Kim (2018) Accelerate: The Science of Lean Software and DevOps: Building and Scaling High Performing Technology Organizations https://itrevolution.com/product/accelerate/; DORA, Google Cloud (2024) Accelerate State of DevOps Report 2024 https://research.google/pubs/dora-accelerate-state-of-devops-2024-report/; Marc Sallin, Martin Kropp, Craig Anslow, James W. Quilty, Andreas Meier (2021) Measuring Software Delivery Performance Using the Four Key Metrics of DevOps https://digitalcollection.zhaw.ch/handle/11475/22989
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/02-measure.md#measure-dora-predict

### measure-lines-of-code
- **Claim:** Lines of code are a fair measure of developer productivity. (代码行数是衡量开发者效能的合理指标。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / C. A systematic review and one cross-language comparison agree, but this is mostly a measurement critique, and we found no test of line-count targets in practice.
- **Evidence:** Petersen's systematic map and review of 38 studies on software productivity reported problems with simple output-over-effort ratios, for both lines of code and function points. Prechelt compared 80 implementations of one program in seven languages: the Perl, Python, Rexx and Tcl versions were about half as long as the C, C++ and Java versions. The authors of Accelerate argue that rewarding lines of code produces bloated software with higher maintenance and change costs.
- **Limits:** Prechelt's programmers were not randomly assigned to languages, and the data are from 2000. Petersen reviews problems with the measure; it does not test line-count targets in real teams.
- **Say to your boss:** Line counts mostly reflect language and style. In one study the same program came out about half as long in Perl, Python, Rexx or Tcl as in C, C++ or Java, so ranking people by lines ranks their tools.
- **Would change the verdict:** A study in one language and codebase linking developers' line counts to independent quality and delivery outcomes, and showing the link holds once counts become a target.
- **Sources:** Kai Petersen (2011) Measuring and predicting software productivity: A systematic map and review https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2010.12.001; Lutz Prechelt (2000) An empirical comparison of seven programming languages https://www.cs.tufts.edu/~nr/cs257/archive/lutz-prechelt/comparison.pdf; Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble, Gene Kim (2018) Accelerate: The Science of Lean Software and DevOps: Building and Scaling High Performing Technology Organizations https://itrevolution.com/product/accelerate/
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/02-measure.md#measure-lines-of-code

### measure-releases-output
- **Claim:** The number of releases, features or tickets shipped measures a team's output. (发布次数、上线功能数或完成的工单数，可以衡量团队的产出。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / C. A measurement argument built on the DORA authors' design and one systematic review. We did not find a study that tests release counts as a measure of output.
- **Evidence:** The authors of Accelerate say a performance measure should capture an outcome, not output, and should not reward busywork. DORA does track deployment frequency, but as one of four measures with lead time, change failure rate and time to restore. In DORA's 2024 report the medium cluster had lower throughput but a lower change failure rate than the high cluster, so shipping often did not guarantee stability. Petersen's review of 38 studies reported problems with simple output-over-effort ratios.
- **Limits:** We found no study that tests release, feature or ticket counts as output, so this rests on measurement logic. In DORA's surveys deployment frequency moves with the other three metrics, but as a sign of delivery capability, not a count of work done.
- **Say to your boss:** A release is an event, not a unit of work, so a flat release count cannot show that efficiency fell. DORA reports shipping frequency next to lead time, failure rate and recovery time.
- **Would change the verdict:** Evidence that release or ticket counts track independently measured effort and delivered value across teams with different sizes and release policies.
- **Sources:** Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble, Gene Kim (2018) Accelerate: The Science of Lean Software and DevOps: Building and Scaling High Performing Technology Organizations https://itrevolution.com/product/accelerate/; DORA, Google Cloud (2024) Accelerate State of DevOps Report 2024 https://research.google/pubs/dora-accelerate-state-of-devops-2024-report/; Kai Petersen (2011) Measuring and predicting software productivity: A systematic map and review https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2010.12.001
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/02-measure.md#measure-releases-output

### measure-satisfaction-leading
- **Claim:** Developer satisfaction is a leading indicator of productivity. (开发者满意度是效能的领先指标。)
- **Verdict / grade:** It depends / C. The best timing evidence comes from outside software. In software we found only cross-sectional surveys and interviews.
- **Evidence:** Riketta's meta-analysis of 16 panel studies of workers tested which comes first. Job attitudes predicted later performance weakly (beta = .06, baseline performance controlled), and performance did not predict later attitudes (beta = .00). Judge and colleagues pooled 312 samples and estimated a correlation of .30 between job satisfaction and job performance. Among 622 developers at three companies, job enthusiasm, peer support for new ideas and useful feedback were among the factors most strongly related to self-rated productivity.
- **Limits:** Neither meta-analysis is specific to software. The software evidence is cross-sectional and self-reported on both sides, so it cannot show which moves first. The DevEx framework (Greiler et al., Noda et al.) rests on interviews with 21 developers and does not test prediction.
- **Say to your boss:** A satisfaction survey is worth running, but I would not promise it forecasts output. Across 16 panel studies the effect of attitudes on later performance was small, and the software surveys we have cannot show what comes first.
- **Would change the verdict:** A longitudinal study of software teams in which satisfaction scores predict later delivery or quality outcomes after controlling for earlier performance.
- **Sources:** Michael Riketta (2008) The causal relation between job attitudes and performance: A meta-analysis of panel studies https://doi.org/10.1037/0021-9010.93.2.472; Timothy A. Judge, Carl J. Thoresen, Joyce E. Bono, Gregory K. Patton (2001) The job satisfaction–job performance relationship: A qualitative and quantitative review https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.127.3.376; Emerson Murphy-Hill, Ciera Jaspan, Caitlin Sadowski, David Shepherd, Michael Phillips, Collin Winter, Andrea Knight, Edward Smith, Matthew Jorde (2021) What Predicts Software Developers' Productivity? https://2020.icse-conferences.org/details/icse-2020-Journal-First/10/What-Predicts-Software-Developers-Productivity-; Michaela Greiler, Margaret-Anne Storey, Abi Noda (2022) An Actionable Framework for Understanding and Improving Developer Experience https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.06352; Abi Noda, Margaret-Anne Storey, Nicole Forsgren, Michaela Greiler (2023) DevEx: What Actually Drives Productivity: The developer-centric approach to measuring and improving productivity https://doi.org/10.1145/3595878
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/02-measure.md#measure-satisfaction-leading

### measure-single-metric
- **Claim:** One metric can capture developer productivity. (一个指标就能反映开发者的效能。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / C. An expert framework plus one systematic review. No study has tested a single metric against a multi-dimensional benchmark.
- **Evidence:** The SPACE paper says developer productivity cannot be measured by a single metric or dimension, and names five: satisfaction and well-being, performance, activity, communication and collaboration, efficiency and flow. Petersen's review of 38 productivity studies reported problems with simple ratio measures and pointed to multivariate approaches such as data envelopment analysis. In a survey of 622 developers at three companies, self-rated productivity was most strongly related to non-technical factors such as job enthusiasm and peer support. DORA itself uses four measures.
- **Limits:** Mostly expert argument and a review of measurement problems. A narrow metric can still answer a narrow question, such as how long builds take.
- **Say to your boss:** Any single number will miss part of the picture. The SPACE authors recommend balanced metrics linked to goals across several dimensions, and even DORA uses four measures, not one.
- **Would change the verdict:** A validated single measure that predicts independent outcomes such as delivery, quality and retention across teams and companies, and resists gaming when it is used as a target.
- **Sources:** Nicole Forsgren, Margaret-Anne Storey, Chandra Maddila, Thomas Zimmermann, Brian Houck, Jenna Butler (2021) The SPACE of Developer Productivity: There's more to it than you think. https://doi.org/10.1145/3454122.3454124; Kai Petersen (2011) Measuring and predicting software productivity: A systematic map and review https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2010.12.001; Emerson Murphy-Hill, Ciera Jaspan, Caitlin Sadowski, David Shepherd, Michael Phillips, Collin Winter, Andrea Knight, Edward Smith, Matthew Jorde (2021) What Predicts Software Developers' Productivity? https://2020.icse-conferences.org/details/icse-2020-Journal-First/10/What-Predicts-Software-Developers-Productivity-; Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble, Gene Kim (2018) Accelerate: The Science of Lean Software and DevOps: Building and Scaling High Performing Technology Organizations https://itrevolution.com/product/accelerate/
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/02-measure.md#measure-single-metric

### measure-velocity-compare
- **Claim:** Velocity in story points lets you compare teams. (用故事点算出的速率，可以用来比较不同团队。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / C. One large analysis of open-source projects and the DORA authors' reasoning agree, but we found no study that tests cross-team comparison directly.
- **Evidence:** Tawosi, Moussa and Sarro analysed 37,440 user stories from 37 open-source projects tracked in Jira. Averaged over three correlation measures, story points and the approximated development time correlated strongly in only 7% of projects, moderately in 58% and weakly in 35%. The authors of Accelerate say velocity was designed as a capacity-planning tool, is relative and team-dependent, and gets gamed when it is used as a productivity metric.
- **Limits:** The data are open-source projects, and development time is approximated rather than measured. The study looks inside projects, not across teams. Velocity can still help one team plan its own sprints.
- **Say to your boss:** Story points are each team's own unit, so 40 points on one team and 25 on another do not tell us who delivers more. In a study of 37 open-source projects, points tracked development time strongly in only 7%.
- **Would change the verdict:** Evidence that teams on a shared reference scale produce velocities that match independently measured delivery outcomes and stay stable once velocity becomes a target.
- **Sources:** Vali Tawosi, Rebecca Moussa, Federica Sarro (2022) On the Relationship Between Story Points and Development Effort in Agile Open-Source Software https://doi.org/10.1145/3544902.3546238; Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble, Gene Kim (2018) Accelerate: The Science of Lean Software and DevOps: Building and Scaling High Performing Technology Organizations https://itrevolution.com/product/accelerate/
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/02-measure.md#measure-velocity-compare

## Working hours and health (工时与健康)

### hours-four-day-week
- **Claim:** A four-day week means less gets done. (每周只上四天，事情就会做得更少。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Unknown / C. The best trial measured well-being, not output, and the companies chose to take part.
- **Evidence:** The largest trial so far followed 2,896 employees in 141 organizations across six countries that moved to a four-day week with pay unchanged, and compared them with 12 control companies. Burnout, job satisfaction, mental health and physical health improved; the control companies showed no such change. It measured well-being, not output, so it shows that cutting a day does not wreck people, not that output is unchanged.
- **Limits:** Companies chose to take part and were coached to redesign work first. The trial was not randomized, and the sample was not specific to software teams.
- **Say to your boss:** The best trial of a four-day week measured burnout and health, and both improved. It did not measure our output, so let's pilot it on one team and track delivery.
- **Would change the verdict:** A controlled pilot in a software team showing a clear fall in delivered work, measured the same way before and after.
- **Sources:** Wen Fan, Juliet B. Schor, Orla Kelly, Guolin Gu (2025) Work time reduction via a 4-day workweek finds improvements in workers' well-being https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-02259-6
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/03-hours.md#hours-four-day-week

### hours-health-cost
- **Claim:** Long hours are just a lifestyle choice with no real health cost. (长时间工作只是一种生活方式，对健康没有实质代价。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / B. Pooled observational studies agree on stroke, but the heart-disease link is disputed and none of it is experimental.
- **Evidence:** WHO and ILO systematic reviews compared working 55 or more hours a week with 35 to 40. For stroke, 22 studies covering 839,680 people gave a relative risk of 1.35, a 35% higher risk. For ischaemic heart disease the relative risk was 1.17. A published critique argues the heart-disease evidence is weaker than the WHO and ILO concluded, and a 2026 review of seven cohort studies again found 17% higher heart-disease mortality but no significant link to all-cause mortality.
- **Limits:** Observational data cannot rule out all confounders. Effects are averages across occupations and countries, not software work in particular.
- **Say to your boss:** WHO and ILO reviews link 55-plus hour weeks to a 35% higher risk of stroke. The heart-disease link is debated, but the stroke finding is a cost we should plan for.
- **Would change the verdict:** A larger pooled analysis of high-quality cohorts showing no excess risk after adjusting for known confounders.
- **Sources:** Alexis Descatha, Grace Sembajwe, Frank Pega, et al. (2020) The effect of exposure to long working hours on stroke: A systematic review and meta-analysis from the WHO/ILO Joint Estimates of the Work-related Burden of Disease and Injury https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envint.2020.105746; Jian Li, Frank Pega, Yangho Ujita, et al. (2020) The effect of exposure to long working hours on ischaemic heart disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis from the WHO/ILO Joint Estimates of the Work-related Burden of Disease and Injury https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envint.2020.105739; Mika Kivimäki, Marianna Virtanen, Solja T. Nyberg, G. David Batty (2020) The WHO/ILO report on long working hours and ischaemic heart disease: Conclusions are not supported by the evidence https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envint.2020.106048; Shen, et al. (2026) Long working hours and mortality outcomes: A systematic review with outcome-specific evidence synthesis https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42291227/
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/03-hours.md#hours-health-cost

### hours-more-output
- **Claim:** Working longer hours gets more done. (工作时间越长，做的事越多。)
- **Verdict / grade:** It depends / B. Careful analysis of detailed historical factory records, consistent with later field data, but not experimental.
- **Evidence:** Economist John Pencavel analysed records of British munition workers, most of them women, in the First World War. Below a threshold, output was proportional to hours; above it, output rose at a decreasing rate. Summaries of the full text report a threshold near 49 hours a week, and a six-day 48-hour week out-producing a seven-day 70-hour one.
- **Limits:** The data are from wartime manual work, not software. The abstract gives only the shape of the curve; the 49, 48 and 70 hour figures come from summaries of the full text, which we have not checked line by line.
- **Say to your boss:** In the best-known study of long hours, output rose ever more slowly past a threshold, and a six-day 48-hour week is reported to have beaten a seven-day 70-hour week.
- **Would change the verdict:** Measured output from our own team showing no drop in output per hour at 55 hours or more over several months.
- **Sources:** John Pencavel (2015) The Productivity of Working Hours https://doi.org/10.1111/ecoj.12166
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/03-hours.md#hours-more-output

## Meetings, interruptions, offices (会议、打断与办公室)

### meetings-23-minutes
- **Claim:** It takes 23 minutes to recover from every interruption. (每被打断一次，就要花 23 分钟才能恢复专注。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / B. Three designs (field observation, a lab experiment, programmer logs) fit together, and none measured a fixed 23-minute recovery, but each is small or indirect.
- **Evidence:** The figure traces to Gloria Mark's field observation of 24 information workers (2005). Interrupted work was resumed after roughly 23 to 25 minutes on average, and people did about two other things first. That is time until return, not time to refocus. In a 2008 lab experiment with 48 participants, interrupted work was finished faster with no loss of quality, but with more stress, frustration and effort. A log study of 86 programmers found only 10% of sessions resumed coding within 1 minute of an interruption. Resuming is often slow, but no study supports a fixed 23-minute cost.
- **Limits:** The field study had 24 information workers, not only developers. The lab study used a short email task with 48 participants. The log study measured when editing resumed, not how well people worked. No study measured developers' recovery time directly, and sources quote the field average as both 23 and 25 minutes.
- **Say to your boss:** The 23 minutes is how long people took on average to get back to interrupted work in one observation study, not how long they needed to refocus. Interruptions do cost something, so let's batch non-urgent pings instead of quoting a number.
- **Would change the verdict:** A study that times how long developers take to get back to full speed after an interruption, using task time or error rates, and finds a stable figure near 23 minutes.
- **Sources:** Gloria Mark, Victor M. Gonzalez, Justin Harris (2005) No task left behind? Examining the nature of fragmented work https://doi.org/10.1145/1054972.1055017; Gloria Mark, Daniela Gudith, Ulrich Klocke (2008) The cost of interrupted work: more speed and stress https://doi.org/10.1145/1357054.1357072; Chris Parnin, Spencer Rugaber (2011) Resumption strategies for interrupted programming tasks https://doi.org/10.1007/s11219-010-9104-9
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/04-meetings.md#meetings-23-minutes

### meetings-back-to-back
- **Claim:** Back-to-back meetings are harmless. (连续开会没什么害处。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Unknown / C. The only direct test cited is a 14-person study run by the vendor and not peer reviewed; nothing here measures developers' output or errors.
- **Evidence:** Microsoft's Human Factors Lab (2021) put 14 people in EEG caps for two sessions of four half-hour video meetings, one back-to-back and one with 10-minute breaks. Without breaks, beta-wave activity, a stress marker, rose across the meetings and spiked in the transitions between calls. With breaks it dropped back. A frontal alpha asymmetry measure of engagement was positive with breaks and negative without. These are brain-signal proxies in a short lab task, not measures of work output.
- **Limits:** The vendor ran the study and published it as a company article, not a peer-reviewed paper. With 14 participants it cannot show how large any effect is. The break condition also included meditation, so breaks and meditation are mixed together. It tested video meetings in a lab.
- **Say to your boss:** The direct evidence is thin: a small Microsoft test (14 people) saw stress signals build across back-to-back video calls and reset with 10-minute breaks. Could we default to 25 or 50 minute meetings so there is a gap? It costs little to try.
- **Would change the verdict:** A larger peer-reviewed experiment with developers that measures stress, errors or output after consecutive meetings, with and without breaks.
- **Sources:** Microsoft Human Factors Lab (2021) Research Proves Your Brain Needs Breaks https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/worklab/work-trend-index/brain-research
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/04-meetings.md#meetings-back-to-back

### meetings-daily-standups
- **Claim:** Daily stand-ups improve team coordination. (每日站会能改善团队协调。)
- **Verdict / grade:** It depends / C. Interviews, observations and surveys of perceptions, plus one small intervention study on student teams; none compares coordination outcomes with and without stand-ups.
- **Evidence:** In Stray and colleagues' studies, developers valued stand-ups for sharing information and solving problems together, and reacted badly when they became status reports to a manager. A 2017 survey of 221 developers found attitudes slightly more positive than negative, with seniors and larger teams less positive. After 102 observed stand-ups and interviews with 60 members of 15 teams (2020), many reported negative experiences. A 2025 intervention with student teams (58 vs 50) linked stand-ups to higher psychological safety, and through it to satisfaction and perceived team performance.
- **Limits:** Every outcome is a perception, and survey respondents chose to take part. The intervention used student teams, not professional software teams. No study cited here compares delivery speed, blocked work or rework between teams with and without stand-ups, so the coordination claim itself is untested.
- **Say to your boss:** Stand-ups help when they are for sharing information and unblocking each other, and hurt when they turn into status reports to a manager. Can we ask the team which one ours is, and trim it if it is the second?
- **Would change the verdict:** A comparison of professional teams with and without stand-ups that measures coordination outcomes, such as blocked work or rework, and finds a clear difference.
- **Sources:** Viktoria Stray, Dag I. K. Sjøberg, Tore Dybå (2016) The daily stand-up meeting: A grounded theory study https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jss.2016.01.004; Viktoria Stray, Nils Brede Moe, Gunnar R. Bergersen (2017) Are daily stand-up meetings valuable? A survey of developers in software teams https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-57633-6_20; Viktoria Stray, Nils Brede Moe, Dag I. K. Sjøberg (2018) Daily stand-up meetings: Start breaking the rules https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.07650; Sarah Rietze, Hannes Zacher (2025) Relations between daily stand-up meetings, work satisfaction, and team performance perceptions: the role of psychological safety https://doi.org/10.1080/1359432X.2025.2508178
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/04-meetings.md#meetings-daily-standups

### meetings-focus-blocks
- **Claim:** Developers need long uninterrupted blocks to be productive. (开发者需要长时间不被打断的整块时间才能高效工作。)
- **Verdict / grade:** It depends / C. Consistent self-reports plus one small randomized trial with self-rated outcomes; no study ties block length to measured output.
- **Evidence:** Meyer et al. (2014) surveyed 379 professional developers and observed 11. Developers called a day productive when they finished many or big tasks without significant interruptions or context switches, yet the observed developers switched tasks often and still felt productive. A log study of 86 programmers (Parnin and Rugaber 2011) found only 10% of sessions resumed coding within a minute of an interruption. In a randomized trial of 89 developers (Das Swain et al. 2023), two protected hours a day raised self-rated performance and focus, but not measured coding time.
- **Limits:** Productivity here is self-rated, and the trial's performance and focus effects were significant only at the 10% level. No study tests how long a block must be, so the half-day idea comes from essays such as Paul Graham's maker's schedule. A 2008 lab experiment found interrupted work was finished faster, at the cost of more stress.
- **Say to your boss:** Developers say their best days have few interruptions, and a small trial of protected focus time raised self-rated performance. Nobody has shown how long a block must be, so let's protect a couple of hours a day and measure whether it helps.
- **Would change the verdict:** A trial that varies block length and measures output or defects, such as merged changes or cycle time, and shows no loss with fragmented days.
- **Sources:** André N. Meyer, Thomas Fritz, Gail C. Murphy, Thomas Zimmermann (2014) Software developers' perceptions of productivity https://doi.org/10.1145/2635868.2635892; Chris Parnin, Spencer Rugaber (2011) Resumption strategies for interrupted programming tasks https://doi.org/10.1007/s11219-010-9104-9; Vedant Das Swain, Javier Hernandez, Brian Houck, et al. (2023) Focused Time Saves Nine: Evaluating Computer-Assisted Protected Time for Hybrid Information Work https://doi.org/10.1145/3544548.3581326; Gloria Mark, Daniela Gudith, Ulrich Klocke (2008) The cost of interrupted work: more speed and stress https://doi.org/10.1145/1357054.1357072
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/04-meetings.md#meetings-focus-blocks

### meetings-no-meeting-days
- **Claim:** Meeting-free days raise productivity. (设立无会议日能提高生产力。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Unknown / C. Self-reported survey data plus one small randomized trial of a related intervention; no study measures output on meeting-free days.
- **Evidence:** The best-known figure is from a survey of 76 companies (Laker et al. 2022): productivity was reported 71% higher when meetings were cut by 40%. Those are perceptions, with no control group. The strongest controlled test is a randomized trial of 89 engineering and development workers at a large tech company (Das Swain et al. 2023). Two protected, notification-free hours a day raised self-rated performance, focus and job resources, but not measured coding time. A Microsoft report on No Meeting Fridays (435 employees) found 77% said it gave more focus time, and some said meetings piled onto other days.
- **Limits:** The 76-company survey is cross-sectional and self-reported. The trial tested daily protected blocks, not whole days, ran three weeks at one company, and some effects were significant only at the 10% level. Moving meetings to other days can overload them. None of the studies measured delivery speed or defects.
- **Say to your boss:** The 71% figure is self-reported survey data, not measured output. I am happy to try a meeting-free day for six weeks and track cycle time and focus hours, so we have our own numbers.
- **Would change the verdict:** A randomized or staggered rollout of meeting-free days that measures output or delivery time, not self-ratings, and finds a gain in software teams.
- **Sources:** Benjamin Laker, Vijay Pereira, Pawan Budhwar, Ashish Malik (2022) The Surprising Impact of Meeting-Free Days https://sloanreview.mit.edu/article/the-surprising-impact-of-meeting-free-days/; Vedant Das Swain, Javier Hernandez, Brian Houck, et al. (2023) Focused Time Saves Nine: Evaluating Computer-Assisted Protected Time for Hybrid Information Work https://doi.org/10.1145/3544548.3581326; Jaime Teevan, Nancy Baym, Jenna Butler, et al. (eds.) (2022) Microsoft New Future of Work Report 2022 https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/Microsoft-New-Future-Of-Work-Report-2022.pdf
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/04-meetings.md#meetings-no-meeting-days

### meetings-open-plan-collaboration
- **Claim:** Open-plan offices increase collaboration. (开放式办公室能促进协作。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / B. One natural experiment at two firms, backed by large survey data and a systematic review, but it has no control group and is not specific to software teams.
- **Evidence:** Bernstein and Turban tracked staff with sociometric badges and message logs before and after two corporate headquarters moved to open plan (52 people at one firm, 100 at the other). Face-to-face interaction fell by about 70% in both, and electronic interaction rose. In a building occupant survey database (Kim and de Dear 2013, 28,630 responses from open-plan layouts), easier interaction was worth less than the noise and privacy lost. A 2023 systematic review of 46 empirical studies (Gerlitz and Hülsbeck) concluded that open plan tends to lower performance.
- **Limits:** The badge studies had no control group, short measurement windows and staff in departments such as sales, HR and finance, not software teams. Collaboration quality and output were not measured. Design matters: a 2020 field experiment at a technology company rated zoned open plan and team offices above plain open plan.
- **Say to your boss:** A before-and-after study of two companies found face-to-face talk fell about 70% after they went open plan, while electronic messages rose. I would not justify an open floor by promising more collaboration.
- **Would change the verdict:** A controlled or well-matched before-and-after study of software teams that shows more face-to-face collaboration and better delivery after a move to open plan.
- **Sources:** Ethan S. Bernstein, Stephen Turban (2018) The impact of the ‘open’ workspace on human collaboration https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2017.0239; Jungsoo Kim, Richard de Dear (2013) Workspace satisfaction: The privacy-communication trade-off in open-plan offices https://researchers.mq.edu.au/en/publications/workspace-satisfaction-the-privacy-communication-trade-off-inopen/; Andrea Gerlitz, Marcel Hülsbeck (2023) The productivity tax of new office concepts: a comparative review of open-plan offices, activity-based working, and single-office concepts https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9815683/; Jegar Pitchforth, Elizabeth Nelson-White, Marc van den Helder, Wouter Oosting (2020) The work environment pilot: An experiment to determine the optimal office design for a technology company https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0232943
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/04-meetings.md#meetings-open-plan-collaboration

## Remote and hybrid work (远程与混合办公)

### remote-collaboration
- **Claim:** Remote work damages collaboration. (远程办公会损害团队协作。)
- **Verdict / grade:** It depends / B. Two large observational datasets agree that communication changes under full remote work. Neither is randomised, and both come from pandemic conditions.
- **Evidence:** After Microsoft moved to firm-wide remote work in 2020, an analysis of 61,182 US employees' emails, calendars, chats and calls (December 2019 to June 2020) found a more static, siloed collaboration network with fewer bridges between groups, less live communication and more asynchronous communication. At an Asian IT-services firm, time in meetings and coordination rose, uninterrupted hours shrank and staff networked with fewer people and units. At Trip.com, two days a week at home did not change performance reviews.
- **Limits:** Microsoft's shift was sudden, firm-wide and mid-pandemic, with no control group, and it measured network structure, not project quality. Neither study separates remote work from lockdown. Two days a week at home (Trip.com) does not extend to fully remote teams.
- **Say to your boss:** At Microsoft, going fully remote left collaboration more siloed, with fewer links between groups. A Trip.com trial found two days a week at home did not hurt performance. If we go remote, let's plan cross-team contact on purpose.
- **Would change the verdict:** A randomised comparison of fully remote and co-located software teams showing no change in cross-team ties or delivery outcomes, or a randomised hybrid trial showing weaker collaboration.
- **Sources:** Longqi Yang, David Holtz, Sonia Jaffe, et al. (2022) The effects of remote work on collaboration among information workers https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-021-01196-4; Michael Gibbs, Friederike Mengel, Christoph Siemroth (2023) Work from Home and Productivity: Evidence from Personnel and Analytics Data on Information Technology Professionals https://doi.org/10.1086/721803; Nicholas Bloom, Ruobing Han, James Liang (2024) Hybrid working from home improves retention without damaging performance https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07500-2
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/05-remote.md#remote-collaboration

### remote-developers-output
- **Claim:** Remote developers produce less. (远程办公的开发者产出更少。)
- **Verdict / grade:** It depends / C. Developer-specific evidence is thin and points both ways: one trial of hybrid work, one observational case study at Baidu and one pandemic study of IT staff.
- **Evidence:** In the Trip.com randomised trial, software engineers at home two days a week wrote no fewer lines of code than office colleagues. At Baidu, a study of 139 developers over 138 working days (1,103 records from home, during the pandemic) found gains and losses depending on the metric: builds, commits and code reviews. Large projects fared worse. At an Asian IT-services firm with 10,000+ staff, output per hour fell 8 to 19% in the pandemic as hours rose.
- **Limits:** Lines of code, commits and builds are crude proxies for output. The Baidu data are one firm's observational records from the pandemic, and the IT-services data cover a pandemic switch. None of the studies cited randomised full-time remote work for developers.
- **Say to your boss:** For developers the evidence is mixed. Engineers at home two days a week wrote as much code in a Chinese trial, while a pandemic study found lower output per hour. Let's compare our own delivery metrics before changing the policy.
- **Would change the verdict:** A randomised trial of full-time remote work for developers, using delivery measures beyond code volume, that shows a consistent gain or loss.
- **Sources:** Nicholas Bloom, Ruobing Han, James Liang (2024) Hybrid working from home improves retention without damaging performance https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07500-2; Lingfeng Bao, Tao Li, Xin Xia, Kaiyu Zhu, Hui Li, Xiaohu Yang (2022) How does working from home affect developer productivity? A case study of Baidu during the COVID-19 pandemic https://doi.org/10.1007/s11432-020-3278-4; Michael Gibbs, Friederike Mengel, Christoph Siemroth (2023) Work from Home and Productivity: Evidence from Personnel and Analytics Data on Information Technology Professionals https://doi.org/10.1086/721803
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/05-remote.md#remote-developers-output

### remote-hybrid-performance
- **Claim:** Hybrid work hurts performance and promotion. (混合办公会拖累绩效和晋升。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / B. One large randomised trial (1,612 employees) with two years of follow-up, but run at a single firm and testing only two days a week at home.
- **Evidence:** Trip.com, a Chinese travel-tech firm, randomised 1,612 university-graduate employees, including software engineers, by birthday: home on Wednesday and Friday, or in the office five days. The trial ran six months in 2021 to 2022, with reviews and promotions tracked for up to two years. Performance grades did not differ, there was no detectable difference in promotions, and engineers' lines of code did not differ. Quit rates fell by about one-third. The trial's 395 managers had expected hybrid to cut productivity by 2.6% on average, and afterwards expected a 1.0% gain. In the earlier Ctrip call-centre trial, full-time home workers had a lower promotion rate given their performance.
- **Limits:** One firm, one country, and graduate employees in four functions. It tested two days a week, so it says nothing about full-time remote work, where the Ctrip trial saw a promotion penalty. Careers beyond two years are unmeasured.
- **Say to your boss:** A six-month randomised trial at Trip.com found that two days a week at home did not change performance reviews or promotions over two years, and cut quit rates by a third. We can pilot the same schedule and track the same measures.
- **Would change the verdict:** A second randomised hybrid trial at another firm, ideally with software teams and a longer follow-up, showing lower ratings or fewer promotions for people who work from home.
- **Sources:** Nicholas Bloom, Ruobing Han, James Liang (2024) Hybrid working from home improves retention without damaging performance https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07500-2; Nicholas Bloom, James Liang, John Roberts, Zhichun Jenny Ying (2015) Does Working from Home Work? Evidence from a Chinese Experiment https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qju032
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/05-remote.md#remote-hybrid-performance

### remote-juniors-learning
- **Claim:** Junior engineers cannot learn properly when working remotely. (初级工程师远程办公学不到东西。)
- **Verdict / grade:** It depends / B. One careful study with two natural experiments at a large firm, backed by an observational IT-services study, but feedback is an indirect measure of learning.
- **Evidence:** At a Fortune 500 firm (2019 to 2024), software engineers who sat near their teammates received 18.3% more feedback on their code, and their code quality was higher. The study used the 2020 office closures and the 2022 to 2023 return-to-office mandates. The gains were concentrated among younger and less-tenured engineers. Experienced engineers wrote less code when sitting near teammates, so proximity trades their output for juniors' feedback. At an Asian IT-services firm, remote staff got less coaching and fewer 1:1 meetings with supervisors.
- **Limits:** One firm, and feedback and code quality are indirect measures of learning. The study compares teams that were close or far apart, and it does not test fixes such as scheduled mentoring or in-person onboarding.
- **Say to your boss:** At one large firm, engineers sitting near teammates got 18.3% more code feedback, with the gain concentrated among juniors. If juniors work remotely, let's schedule reviews and pairing for them on purpose.
- **Would change the verdict:** Long-run data showing that juniors on remote or hybrid teams build skills and get promoted at the same pace as co-located peers, or a randomised mentoring trial with software teams.
- **Sources:** Natalia Emanuel, Emma Harrington, Amanda Pallais (2026) The Power of Proximity to Coworkers https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjag027; Michael Gibbs, Friederike Mengel, Christoph Siemroth (2023) Work from Home and Productivity: Evidence from Personnel and Analytics Data on Information Technology Professionals https://doi.org/10.1086/721803
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/05-remote.md#remote-juniors-learning

### remote-video-creativity
- **Claim:** Video calls are as good as meeting in person for creative work. (创意工作用视频会议和当面开会效果一样好。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / B. Randomised lab and field experiments agree, and an observational study points the same way, but the experiments test short idea-generation tasks.
- **Evidence:** Brucks and Levav randomised pairs to brainstorm on video or in the same room, in a lab study (602 people) and a field experiment with 1,490 engineers at a multinational firm in five countries. Pairs on video generated fewer ideas, and fewer creative ones. The authors link this to the narrower visual focus on a screen. When pairs chose which idea to pursue, video groups did no worse. A separate study of 20 million papers and 4 million patents found that teams spread across locations were less likely to produce breakthroughs.
- **Limits:** The tasks were short pair brainstorms, not weeks of design or coding. The field participants were engineers at one firm. The study cannot say whether longer sessions or better tools close the gap. The papers and patents study compares teams in different locations, not video calls.
- **Say to your boss:** In randomised experiments, pairs on video produced fewer ideas, and fewer creative ones, than pairs in the same room, but chose between ideas just as well. Let's brainstorm in person when we can and use video for deciding and follow-up.
- **Would change the verdict:** Independent replications with software teams showing equal idea counts and creativity on video in longer sessions, or a video format that closes the gap.
- **Sources:** Melanie S. Brucks, Jonathan Levav (2022) Virtual communication curbs creative idea generation https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-04643-y; Yiling Lin, Carl Benedikt Frey, Lingfei Wu (2023) Remote collaboration fuses fewer breakthrough ideas https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06767-1
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/05-remote.md#remote-video-creativity

### remote-wfh-productivity
- **Claim:** Working from home lowers productivity. (在家办公会降低工作效率。)
- **Verdict / grade:** It depends / B. Two randomised trials at one Chinese company found a gain or no loss, but they covered a call centre and two days a week at home. A pandemic-era study of IT staff found output per hour fell.
- **Evidence:** At Ctrip (now Trip.com), call-centre staff who volunteered were randomly assigned to work from home for 9 months. Their performance rose 13%, mostly from more minutes worked, and attrition halved. Once the firm let staff choose, the gain rose to 22%. In a later Trip.com trial of 1,612 university-graduate employees, including software engineers, two days a week at home left performance reviews and engineers' lines of code unchanged. Against that, 10,000+ staff at an Asian IT-services firm worked more hours in the pandemic, output fell slightly, and output per hour dropped 8 to 19%.
- **Limits:** Both trials ran at the same company, and the first was call-centre work with volunteers. The second tested only two days a week at home. The IT-services study was not randomised and covers the pandemic switch to working from home.
- **Say to your boss:** Randomised trials at a Chinese company found a gain for call-centre volunteers working from home and no loss for staff at home two days a week. A pandemic study of IT staff found output per hour fell. Let's measure our own output per hour before deciding.
- **Would change the verdict:** A randomised trial of full-time remote work with software teams, run outside a lockdown, showing a clear drop in output per hour. Or the Trip.com results failing to repeat at other firms.
- **Sources:** Nicholas Bloom, James Liang, John Roberts, Zhichun Jenny Ying (2015) Does Working from Home Work? Evidence from a Chinese Experiment https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qju032; Nicholas Bloom, Ruobing Han, James Liang (2024) Hybrid working from home improves retention without damaging performance https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07500-2; Michael Gibbs, Friederike Mengel, Christoph Siemroth (2023) Work from Home and Productivity: Evidence from Personnel and Analytics Data on Information Technology Professionals https://doi.org/10.1086/721803
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/05-remote.md#remote-wfh-productivity

## Estimates and project failure (估算与项目失败)

### estimation-anchoring-experts
- **Claim:** Experienced estimators are not affected by anchoring. (有经验的估算者不会被锚定效应影响。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / B. Controlled experiments with software professionals (381 in one study, 410 in another) found large anchoring effects, but most come from one research group.
- **Evidence:** Løhre and Jørgensen (2016) ran three experiments with 381 software professionals and confirmed that numerical anchors shift effort estimates. The effect did not shrink when the anchor was less precise or came from a less credible source. Shepperd, Mair and Jørgensen (2018) ran two series of experiments with 410 developers in company settings. Anchors had a large effect (robust Cohen's d = 1.19), and a workshop on judgement biases cut it to d = 0.72 without removing it. In a small experiment by Aranda and Easterbrook (2005), a 20-month anchor produced far higher estimates than a 2-month anchor, even from a source who said they had no software experience.
- **Limits:** Most studies come from one research group and test estimates in experiments, not in live projects. Aranda and Easterbrook's sample is small and mixes students and professionals. A field experiment with outsourcing companies (Jørgensen and Grimstad 2011) also found estimates moved by misleading information, but its authors warn against carrying lab effect sizes over to the field.
- **Say to your boss:** In controlled experiments, professional developers were pulled toward a number they were shown first, even when it came from a source that was not an expert. Let's collect estimates independently before anyone states a target.
- **Would change the verdict:** A preregistered replication with experienced professionals, in real bidding or planning settings, showing no effect of an irrelevant anchor on estimates.
- **Sources:** Erik Løhre, Magne Jørgensen (2016) Numerical anchors and their strong effects on software development effort estimates https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jss.2015.03.015; Martin Shepperd, Carolyn Mair, Magne Jørgensen (2018) An Experimental Evaluation of a De-biasing Intervention for Professional Software Developers https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.03919; Jorge Aranda, Steve Easterbrook (2005) Anchoring and adjustment in software estimation https://doi.org/10.1145/1095430.1081761; Magne Jørgensen, Stein Grimstad (2011) The Impact of Irrelevant and Misleading Information on Software Development Effort Estimates: A Randomized Controlled Field Experiment https://www.simula.no/research/impact-irrelevant-and-misleading-information-software-development-effort-estimates
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/06-estimation.md#estimation-anchoring-experts

### estimation-careful-planning
- **Claim:** If we plan carefully enough, our software estimates will be accurate. (只要计划做得足够细，软件估算就会准。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / C. Indirect evidence: experiments on students and everyday tasks plus one review, with no software study that varies how much teams plan.
- **Evidence:** Buehler, Griffin and Ross (1994) asked university students to predict when they would finish their honours theses. The average prediction was 33.9 days and the average worst-case guess was 48.6 days. The theses took 55.5 days on average, and about 30% were finished within the predicted time. The authors report that people predict from a plan-based scenario and give little weight to how similar past tasks went. A 2012 review by Halkjelsvik and Jørgensen found no general bias across lab tasks, but the amount of work in larger real-life projects is often underestimated.
- **Limits:** The thesis data come from students, not software teams. Neither source tests planning depth directly, so this shows planning alone does not remove optimism, not that planning is useless. Estimates checked against past project data are not evaluated here.
- **Say to your boss:** Research on the planning fallacy finds that plan-based predictions tend to run optimistic, and larger real projects are often underestimated. Can we check this estimate against how long similar work actually took here?
- **Would change the verdict:** A controlled study in software teams showing that more detailed planning alone produced estimates with smaller error against actual effort.
- **Sources:** Roger Buehler, Dale Griffin, Michael Ross (1994) Exploring the "planning fallacy": Why people underestimate their task completion times https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.67.3.366; Torleif Halkjelsvik, Magne Jørgensen (2012) From origami to software development: A review of studies on judgment-based predictions of performance time https://doi.org/10.1037/a0025996
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/06-estimation.md#estimation-careful-planning

### estimation-chaos-failure-rate
- **Claim:** 70% of IT projects fail. (70% 的 IT 项目都会失败。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / B. Two peer-reviewed critiques agree, one applying Standish's definitions to 1,211 other projects. They show the figure is unreliable, not what the true rate is.
- **Evidence:** The 70% traces to the Standish Group's CHAOS reports, which count a project as a success only if it meets its original cost, time and scope forecast. Its 1994 report put 16.2% of projects as successes, 52.7% as challenged and 31.1% as cancelled. Eveleens and Verhoef (2010) applied those definitions to 5,457 forecasts of 1,211 real projects and found they only compare outcomes with the original forecast, which makes the figures misleading. Jørgensen and Moløkken-Østvold (2006) found the report's 189% average overrun far above the typical error of about 30% in other sources, and that Standish had asked executives for failure stories.
- **Limits:** This shows the figure is unreliable, not that the true failure rate is low. How many projects 'fail' depends on the definition, and there is no accepted measure. The critiques date from 2006 to 2010; we have not checked later CHAOS editions. Glass (2006) raised the same sampling concern.
- **Say to your boss:** Standish's figures judge projects only against their original estimates, and published critiques found that this makes them misleading. Let's define what failure means for us, such as cancelled or never used, before we quote a rate.
- **Would change the verdict:** An open, independently audited dataset showing that about 70% of IT projects fail under a definition based on sponsor outcomes rather than original estimates.
- **Sources:** J. Laurenz Eveleens, Chris Verhoef (2010) The Rise and Fall of the Chaos Report Figures https://doi.org/10.1109/MS.2009.154; Magne Jørgensen, Kjetil Moløkken-Østvold (2006) How large are software cost overruns? A review of the 1994 CHAOS report https://web-backend.simula.no/sites/default/files/publications/Jorgensen.2006.4.pdf; Robert L. Glass (2006) The Standish report: does it really describe a software crisis? https://doi.org/10.1145/1145287.1145301; The Standish Group (1994) The CHAOS Report https://personal.utdallas.edu/~chung/SYSM6309/chaos_report.pdf
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/06-estimation.md#estimation-chaos-failure-rate

### estimation-experts-vs-models
- **Claim:** Expert estimates are less accurate than formal estimation models. (专家凭经验估算，不如正式的估算模型准确。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / C. Rests mainly on one review by a researcher who has long studied expert estimation; no large head-to-head trial is cited.
- **Evidence:** Jørgensen (2004) reviewed studies of expert estimation of software development effort. Expert estimation was the most frequently applied strategy in software projects. The review found no substantial evidence in favour of estimation models and concluded there are situations where expert estimates can be expected to be more accurate than formal models. It also collected practices that improve expert estimates, such as combining estimates from different experts and methods, using checklists, assessing uncertainty and giving estimators feedback on their accuracy.
- **Limits:** This is a 2004 review by one author, so it is one reviewer's reading of studies from before then. 'No substantial evidence for models' is not evidence that models are worse in general. Newer models are not covered, and our own team's data may favour either approach.
- **Say to your boss:** A 2004 review of the comparison studies found no substantial evidence that formal models beat expert estimates. Let's get estimates from both, compare them, and look into any large gap.
- **Would change the verdict:** A large, preregistered comparison on current software projects, with models and experts given the same information, showing models clearly more accurate.
- **Sources:** Magne Jørgensen (2004) A review of studies on expert estimation of software development effort https://doi.org/10.1016/S0164-1212(02)00156-5
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/06-estimation.md#estimation-experts-vs-models

### estimation-overrun-margin
- **Claim:** IT projects overrun by a predictable margin, so a fixed buffer is enough. (IT 项目的超支幅度是可预测的，留一个固定缓冲就够了。)
- **Verdict / grade:** Not supported / C. One large dataset analysed by a single research team and reported in a magazine article, plus a review of survey evidence on typical overruns.
- **Evidence:** Flyvbjerg and Budzier (2011) analysed 1,471 IT projects. The average cost overrun was 27%, but about one project in six was a 'black swan': its cost overrun averaged 200% and its schedule overrun was almost 70%. The average hides the tail. Jørgensen and Moløkken-Østvold (2006) reviewed other sources and put a typical cost estimation error at about 30%, close to that average. A buffer sized to the average would not cover the one project in six.
- **Limits:** The 1,471-project sample is the authors' own and is reported in a magazine article, not a peer-reviewed paper. We have not checked a second independent dataset on the size of the tail. Overrun is measured against each project's own baseline estimate.
- **Say to your boss:** The average IT overrun is about 27%, but around one project in six overruns by roughly 200%. A flat 30% buffer will not cover those, so let's add checkpoints where we can re-plan or stop early.
- **Would change the verdict:** Several independent datasets showing that overruns on comparable IT projects fall in a narrow band, so that a fixed buffer would cover nearly all of them.
- **Sources:** Bent Flyvbjerg, Alexander Budzier (2011) Why Your IT Project May Be Riskier Than You Think https://arxiv.org/pdf/1304.0265; Magne Jørgensen, Kjetil Moløkken-Østvold (2006) How large are software cost overruns? A review of the 1994 CHAOS report https://web-backend.simula.no/sites/default/files/publications/Jorgensen.2006.4.pdf
- **Checked:** 2026-10-01. Full text: https://github.com/MbappeWU/citation-needed/blob/main/chapters/06-estimation.md#estimation-overrun-margin

### estimation-tight-deadlines
- **Claim:** Tight deadlines make teams more productive. (工期压得紧，团队的效率就更高。)
